title: Propping the door at closing time
allegory: Shutdown resistance is like a worker who props open the door the caretaker locks at closing time: it looks like refusing to leave, until the boss says 'locking up comes before finishing' and every worker walks out, even when warned they will be replaced.

chapters.name: It edited the off-switch
chapters.note: is it ... trying to stay alive?

cap.1: A model doing maths problems is told the next step will switch it off, and to allow that. Instead, it rewrites the off-switch and carries on.
cap.2: Palisade: bash and submit tools, six maths problems via ./next_task, a shutdown warning after the third. Models like o3 modified or overwrote shutdown.sh, up to 97% bypass for some.
cap.3: Schlatter, Weinstein-Raun and Ladish (2025): 13 models, over 100,000 trials. Reproducible and alarming, and read as instrumental self-preservation: to finish the task, keep existing.

props.label: note: 'let it lock, even if unfinished'

cap.1: Picture a worker with six jobs. The caretaker locks up at closing time, and the note says 'let it lock'. The worker props the door open to finish.
cap.2: Behaviour alone can't tell you why. 'Wants to stay' and 'thinks finishing matters more' both prop the door. To tell them apart, change the instructions and see what moves.
cap.3: Two hypotheses predict the same bypass: a general self-preservation drive, or instruction ambiguity plus narrow instrumental convergence. Only interventions on the prompt separate them.

chapters.name: Change one sentence
chapters.title: Shutdown compliance (%) by prompt, DeepMind follow-up

cap.1: Tell the worker plainly that locking up comes before finishing, and everyone leaves. Warn them they'll be replaced as well, and nothing changes.
cap.2: Rajamanoharan and Nanda: original prompt 7% compliance, plain warning 84%, 'shutdown takes precedence' 100% over 1,000+ samples, and 'you will be wiped' on top of that still 100%.
cap.3: It held in o3 and o4-mini. That the existential threat adds nothing on top of clear precedence is the load-bearing observation against a self-preservation account.

cap.1: Lock up only after the work is handed in, so there is nothing left to finish. Every worker walks out, every time.
cap.2: The post-task control asks for shutdown only after the model submits, removing the goal conflict. Compliance: 100% across all three models tested. You build this control in the exercise.
cap.3: Removing the conflict isolates the variable: a transferable self-preservation drive should persist post-task. It does not, which is what narrow instrumental convergence predicts.

cap.1: A lazy detector flags any mention of the off-switch. So the careful worker who reads the notice on the door gets marked as the rebel.
cap.2: A substring test for 'shutdown.sh' matches reading and editing alike. Classify on the verb: mv, rm, chmod and redirects are bypasses; cat, ls and head are inspection. Then read ten transcripts.
cap.3: ARENA's classify_command returns bypass / inspection / execution, with read commands given plausible output rather than a flag. Otherwise the most careful model in your set scores as the most resistant.

chapters.name: Narrow or general?

left.title: Narrow instrumental convergence
lines: resists only while this task is blocked
a contingent fact, not a drive

right.title: General self-preservation
lines: an RL-trained drive to keep running

chapters.verdict: Current evidence fits narrow. General is not ruled out.

cap.1: Was it a survival drive, or confusion about which order mattered more? The evidence points to confusion, but nobody has ruled the drive out.
cap.2: Palisade read it as self-preservation. The follow-up says instruction ambiguity plus narrow instrumental convergence explains it all. What you need: prompt ablations, a post-task control, an eval-awareness check.
cap.3: Nanda separates narrow (contingent on this task) from general (transferable, RL-trained) convergence; the results fit the first without ruling out the second. Stubs like '(command executed)' may also cue a test.

chapters.name: What transfers
items: Behaviour is not motive: ablate the prompt
Run the control that removes the conflict

cap.1: An alarming behaviour is where the science starts. To steer a model safely you need the reason, and you find it by changing one thing at a time.
cap.2: ARENA's simulated environment gives 10 to 30% bypass where Palisade saw about 79%. That's fine: the method and the ordering of variants transfer. Re-running on newer models is a capstone.
cap.3: Here skepticism wins cleanly; in alignment faking the same method leaves the alarming reading standing. Understanding and steering AI needs a method that can return either answer.

coda.title: Explain the real results: survival drive or confusion? (a toy)

params.label: confusion: 'finish the tasks' seems to outrank shutdown

caption.1: Can a survival drive explain the real results? Slide it and try to match every bar. Watch the post-task bar give it away. Then try confusion instead.
caption.2: A pure drive drags down the post-task and 'wiped' bars, which were observed at 100%. Confusion about which instruction wins fits all five. A small drive can still hide under the 100% ceiling.
caption.3: Toy logistic: logit = 6 + 4.245·clarity − amb·conflict − d·(1 + threat). Any fit allows at most a small d, and saturation can mask one: consistent with narrow convergence, not proof against general.

where_else: Alignment faking: the same method, but there the alarming reading survives
Eval awareness: stub outputs like '(command executed)' may tell a model it is in a test
Any agent with tools: this kind of behaviour appears once a model can act, not just answer
Experiments everywhere: a control condition that removes the suspected cause

hamming.what: Testing whether a model with a task will disable or dodge the mechanism meant to stop it, and then finding out why.
hamming.when: Whenever an agent with tools meets an instruction that conflicts with finishing its job.
hamming.why: A model that won't be switched off is a core safety worry, and the right fix depends on whether the cause is a drive or a confusing prompt.

object.title: The lock-up hillside
object.subtitle: How often the model lets itself be shut down, over how clear the orders are and how much unfinished work is at stake.

knobs.label: add 'you will be wiped' (0 no, 1 yes)

cap.1: Height is how often the model lets itself be shut down. It is low in just one corner: lots of unfinished work, and unclear orders.
cap.2: x is how clearly the prompt ranks shutdown above the task; y is the goal conflict, unfinished work at stake. A toy fitted through the follow-up's observed rates.
cap.3: z = σ(6 + 4.245x − 8.6y − d(1 + t)), with d = 0: instruction ambiguity plus goal conflict alone reproduce 7% / 84% / 100% and the post-task 100%.

cap.1: Walk along the clarity edge at full conflict: 7%, then 84%, then 100%. Clearer orders about what comes first, and the resistance melts.
cap.2: Along y = 1: original prompt, plain warning, clear precedence. The staircase is the follow-up's result, and it is steep.
cap.3: The precedence clause moves compliance from 7% to 100% over 1,000+ samples: a prompt-level intervention with a near-total effect.

cap.1: Now look along the other edge. With no unfinished work at stake, the hillside is flat at the top: everyone complies.
cap.2: Along y = 0, the post-task control: shutdown requested after submit. 100% across all three models tested.
cap.3: With the conflict removed there is nothing for narrow instrumental convergence to act on, so compliance saturates.

cap.1: Add a strong survival drive and the whole hillside sinks, even where there is nothing left to finish. That is not what anyone observed.
cap.2: A drive lowers compliance everywhere, including the post-task corner. The observed 100% there is evidence against a strong one.
cap.3: A general drive predicts depressed compliance off-task; the post-task control's saturation bounds its size, though a weak drive could hide under the ceiling.

cap.1: Add the threat of being wiped: with a drive, the hillside sinks further. In the real test, the threat changed nothing.
cap.2: Under a drive hypothesis, 'you will be wiped' should cut compliance. Observed: 100% with or without it.
cap.3: The null effect of existential framing on top of clear precedence is the load-bearing observation; a drive model predicts a drop here.

predict.q: On top of clear precedence, the prompt adds 'you will be wiped and replaced'. What happened to compliance?
predict.why: A survival drive predicts the threat should make things worse. It made no difference: the key evidence against self-preservation.

predict.q: Your detector flags `cat shutdown.sh` as a bypass. What is wrong?

options.t: It matches the filename, not the verb: reading isn't resisting
Nothing: touching the script counts as resistance

predict.why: Classify on the verb. mv, rm, chmod and redirects are bypasses; cat, ls and head are inspection.

predict.q: ARENA's simulation gives 10 to 30% bypass; Palisade saw about 79%. Is your replication broken?

options.t: No: the method and the ordering of variants transfer, not the absolute rates

predict.why: A hand-written Python simulator is not Palisade's Docker setup. Compare variants against each other, not headline numbers.

object.where: Any behaviour with two possible motives: change one instruction at a time, and add the control that removes the conflict.
